newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan trade outlook rosy for 1997, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan trade outlook rosy for 1997, analysts say.

text.p: Taiwan's trade outlook looks rosy for 1997 with a little help from Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule and strikes in South Korea, analysts said on Tuesday.
Taiwan's exports grew 3.9 percent last year to US$115.98 billion while imports fell 2.2 percent to T$101.28 billion, the Finance Ministry said on Tuesday.
"We expect moderate growth in exports and imports in 1997, each with more than an eight percent rise from 1996," ministry director Hsu Kuo-chung told reporters.
An international economic recovery would help exports while the speeding up of infrastructure projects at home would stimulate imports for raw materials, Hsu added.
Analysts made similar forecasts, projecting growth of seven to nine percent in both exports and imports.

"Expecting Taiwan's 1997 exports to rise more than eight percent is reasonable as global trade is seen to grow some seven percent compared with 5.5 percent in 1996," said Daniel Chen, chief economist at ChinaTrust Commercial Bank.
Chen attributed the poor Taiwan 1996 exports partly to weaker-than-expected 1996 global trade.
"It will need more effort to see eight percent growth in exports, but it's possible," Chen said.

He mentioned rising investment connected to the construction of 11 private power plants, tariff cuts if Taiwan enters the World Trade Organisation in 1997 and rising consumer goods imports triggered by a bullish stock market.
Hong Kong's scheduled return to Chinese rule in July this year should also help trade, analysts said.

"Communist China will focus on constructing Hong Kong, and I am optimistic that it will try to make the Hong Kong-Taiwan link smooth, especially on trade concerns," said Alex Chen, assistance research manager at HSBC James Capel Taiwan.
Chinese war games near the Taiwan Strait ahead of Taiwan's historic presidential elections in March were one of the main reasons for the island's poor trade performance in 1996, analysts said.
"Now that the negative China factor is seen gone in 1997, we can expect a strong domestic recovery both in trade and economy this year," ChinaTrust's Chen said.
South Korea's expanding labour strikes would likely to transfer some orders to Taiwan manufacturers from Seoul, analysts said.
"Orders from South Korea should help Taiwan's exports in the first quarter," Chen said.
Analysts noted rising capital goods imports, which showed a healthy 16 percent year-on-year rise in December, were also an encouraging sign.

"The capital goods imports have for sure built an uptrend since June, and this implies rising domestic investment that can fuel a domestic recovery," said Amy Huang, an economist at Nomura Securities.
Analysts said they expected electronics, Taiwan's star export industry, to remain strong in 1997 and the petrochemical industry to recover in the second half.
